51-029.r: British Indian Association (Calcutta, 1851) → first president Radha Kant Dev; founder members included Debendranath Tagore.

51-030.r: British Indian Association → Radha Kant Dev; Bombay Presidency Association → K.T. Telang; Central Mohammedan National Association → Syed Amir Ali; Servants of India Society → Gokhale.

52-001.r: INC → founded by A.O. Hume, retired ICS civil servant; began as Indian National Union (1884); first session moved from Poona to Bombay (cholera); renamed on Dadabhai Naoroji's advice.

52-005.r: INC → set up 1885; first session Bombay, 28-30 December 1885, Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College; 72 delegates; President W.C. Bonnerjee, General Secretary A.O. Hume.
52-005.h: Bombay 1885: 72 delegates met in a Sanskrit College.

52-014.r: W.C. Bonnerjee's 1885 aims → friendship among patriots, national unity beyond caste/sect/region, presenting public demands. Social issues were kept off the Congress platform.

52-015.r: Early Congress demands → larger, more representative legislative councils, Indians in high posts, separation of judiciary from executive; never their unification.

52-016.r: General Secretary of INC in 1885 → A.O. Hume (organiser); President of the first session → W.C. Bonnerjee.
52-016.t: Don't swap: Hume = General Secretary; Bonnerjee = first President.

52-017.r: INC founded (1885) under Viceroy Lord Dufferin (1884-1888), who ridiculed it as representing a 'microscopic minority'.

52-023.r: Surendranath Banerjee → absent from INC's founding session; he was presiding over the second Indian National Conference in Calcutta, December 1885.

52-024.r: Second INC session → Calcutta, 1886, presided over by Dadabhai Naoroji.

52-025.r: Muslim delegates at INC → 2 in first session; 33 in second (Calcutta, 1886; 436 delegates); 81 in third (1887); 221 in fourth (1888).

52-026.r: British Committee of INC → set up in London, July 1889, President Sir W. Wedderburn; ran weekly journal 'India'.

52-027.r: First Muslim INC President → Badruddin Tyabji, third session, Madras, 27-30 December 1887.

52-030.r: Second Muslim INC President → Rahimtulla M. Sayani, Calcutta session, 1896.
52-030.h: Muslim Presidents in order: Tyabji first, Sayani second.

52-031.r: Only 2 true: first Muslim INC President → Badruddin Tyabji (Madras, 1887). First woman → Annie Besant (Calcutta, 1917); Sarojini Naidu was first Indian woman (Kanpur, 1925).

52-033.r: First European INC President → George Yule, 4th session, 1888.

52-034.r: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan → never linked with Congress; loyal to the British; formed United Indian Patriotic Association with Raja Shiv Prasad.

52-035.r: Bal Gangadhar Tilak → never elected INC President. Of Lal-Bal-Pal only Lala Lajpat Rai presided (Calcutta special session, 1920); Annie Besant first woman President (1917).
52-035.h: Lal-Bal-Pal: only 'Lal' (Lajpat Rai) got the chair.

52-040.r: First woman INC President → Annie Besant, 32nd session, Calcutta, 26-29 December 1917.
52-040.t: Don't confuse with Sarojini Naidu, the first Indian woman President.

52-045.r: First Indian woman INC President → Sarojini Naidu, 40th session, Kanpur, 1925; later first woman Governor of Uttar Pradesh (1947-49).

52-047.r: True: second session under Dadabhai Naoroji (Calcutta, 1886); INC and Muslim League both met at Lucknow, 1916 (Lucknow Pact). False: first session was in Bombay, not Calcutta.

52-048.r: 27th INC session → Bankipur (Patna), 1912, President R.N. Mudholkar; A.O. Hume was called 'father of the Congress' there.

52-050.r: "Swaraj is my birthright, I shall have it" → Tilak, Lucknow session 1916; Extremists rejoined; Lucknow Pact (Congress-League Agreement) through Tilak and Jinnah.

52-055.r: True: C.R. Das acted as President from prison (1921 Ahmedabad session, Hakim Ajmal Khan presided); Alfred Webb President, Madras, 1894. False: Sarojini first woman President; Hume a President.

52-056.r: "Congress Movement was neither inspired by the people, nor devised or planned by them" → Lala Lajpat Rai.

52-057.r: Safety valve theory → Lala Lajpat Rai (in 'Young India') to attack Moderates; called Congress Dufferin's brainchild, meant to protect British rule from threats.

52-059.r: Lord Curzon (1900) → "The Congress is tottering to its fall, and one of my greatest ambitions... is to assist it to a peaceful demise."

52-060.r: Subhash Chandra Bose → as Congress President (Haripura, 1938) advocated Roman script for the Hindi language.

52-061.r: Mahatma Gandhi → suggested winding up the Indian National Congress after India attained independence.

52-062.r: Amritsar session 1919 → N.C. Kelkar and I.B. Sen helped Gandhi write Congress's new Constitution, replacing the busy Tilak and C.R. Das.

52-063.r: Lord Wellington → attended the Bombay Congress session of 1915; he was not Governor-General then (his tenure: 1931-1936).

52-064.r: C. Vijay Raghav Chariar → presided over Nagpur session 1920, where Gandhi's Swaraj through Non-cooperation was accepted.

52-065.r: Nagpur session 1920 → Congress first declared its policy towards Indian (Princely) States, demanding full responsible government for their citizens.

52-066.r: Both true: Nagpur 1920 → Provincial Congress Committees formed on linguistic basis; in 1948 Congress rejected linguistic reorganisation of provinces.

52-067.r: Gaya session 1922 → President Chittaranjan Das (Deshbandhu); defended Aurobindo in Alipore Bomb Case; formed Swaraj Party with Motilal Nehru.

52-070.r: All India Harijan Sevak Sangh → founded by M.K. Gandhi in 1932.

52-071.r: Order of INC Presidents: Gandhi (Belgaum, 1924; his only session) → Sarojini Naidu (Kanpur, 1925) → Nehru (Lahore, 1929) → Patel (Karachi, 1931).

52-075.r: Abul Kalam Azad → Ramgarh 1940; Sarojini Naidu → Kanpur 1925; Motilal Nehru → Amritsar 1919; Rajendra Prasad → Bombay 1934.

52-076.r: INC sessions in U.P.: Banaras → 1905; Lucknow → 1916; Kanpur → 1925; Meerut → 1946.

52-077.r: Nehru → called socialism the key to India's problems in his presidential address, Lucknow session, 1936.

52-078.r: Haripura session (51st, Gujarat, 19-21 February 1938) → Subhas Chandra Bose; National Planning Committee formed here with Jawaharlal Nehru as its head.

52-081.r: Abul Kalam Azad → youngest INC President (Delhi special session, 1923); later President for six years, 1940-46.
52-081.t: Not Nehru: Azad presided in 1923 at a younger age.

52-082.r: M.A. Ansari → Madras (1927); Purushottam Das Tandon → Nasik (1950); Sarojini Naidu → Kanpur (1925); Subhash Chandra Bose → Haripura (1938).

52-083.r: Abul Kalam Azad → INC President for six continuous years, 1940-46 (Quit India period); also youngest President (1923).

52-084.r: J.B. Kripalani → INC President at Independence and Partition; elected November 1946 at Meerut session.

52-086.r: 'Jana Gana Mana' (Rabindranath Tagore) → first sung at Calcutta INC session, 27 December 1911; adopted as National Anthem on 24 January 1950.

52-087.r: Tilak's last INC session → Amritsar, 1919; he advised 'responsive cooperation' with the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms instead of boycott.

53-001.r: All four shaped the pre-Gandhi national movement: Italian-Abyssinian War, Boxer movement (China), Irish revolutionaries, Japan's 1905 win over Russia (greatest impact).
53-001.h: Japan beating Russia broke the myth that the white race was invincible.

53-002.r: Both true: Moderate phase (1885-1905) supported the democratic, scientific culture of modern Europe and strongly criticised the economic side of British imperialism.

53-003.r: Moderates' method → constitutional agitation: faith in British justice, annual sessions, speeches, resolutions and petitions.

53-004.r: Swadeshi Movement → led to the Surat split (1907) into Moderates and Extremists, over resolutions on Swaraj, Swadeshi, National Education and boycott.

53-005.r: Moderate leaders → mostly urban (Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Dinshaw Wacha, W.C. Bonnerjee, S.N. Banerjee); prosperous middle-class professionals.

53-006.r: Dadabhai Naoroji → from 1904 (International Socialist Congress) kept demanding self-rule for India; demanded 'Swaraj' in his 1906 INC presidential address.

53-007.r: G.K. Gokhale → a Moderate leader using constitutional methods, not an extremist.

53-008.r: Gokhale (founder, Servants of India Society) → not an extremist; Bipin Chandra Pal, Lokmanya Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai led extreme nationalism.

53-010.r: Bal Gangadhar Tilak → accused Congress of 'politics of prayer, petition and protest' (the Moderate method).

53-012.r: Congress policy of prayer and petition → ended under Bal Gangadhar Tilak; Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal became his followers.

53-013.r: B.C. Pal → called the Indian National Congress a "Begging Institute".

53-014.r: Both true: Bipin Chandra Pal → Brahmo Samaj leader and social reformer; published the weekly 'New India' (1901).

53-015.r: Extremists dominated the national movement after 1906; Surat split in December 1907. Leaders: Lajpat Rai, Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo Ghosh.

53-016.r: Aurobindo Ghosh → Extremist (Lal, Bal, Pal, Ghose); arrested 1908 (Maniktala garden raid), released for lack of evidence, later moved to Pondicherry.
